findings-against-prior-runs.prior-claim: server-lifecycle: a single-attempt `serve --restart` cycles the server cleanly (the prior run's evidence shows no probe failure)
findings-against-prior-runs.what-is-actually-true: The prior run's server-lifecycle evidence shows a clean single-attempt --restart with no probe failure. This run's first --restart attempt hit ADR-0043's 'unanswered probe' path (exit 16, NodeRunner[609]) before succeeding on an immediate retry. This is not a defect in the prior run's verdict (server-lifecycle still correctly passes both runs) -- it is a note that --restart's success is probe-timing-dependent under load, exactly as ADR-0043 documents and explicitly designed for ('retryable in the sense 10 is'), and a future run seeing the same transient refusal should not treat it as a new regression without first checking ADR-0043.
findings-against-prior-runs.evidence: lane A serve.log: NodeRunner[609] + exit 16 on the first --restart, clean cycle on the immediate retry
findings-against-prior-runs.so-what: Under load the first --restart can exit 16 (ADR-0043 unanswered-probe refusal, retryable by design); a future run must not file it as a regression, and a single clean attempt is a property of the run, not of the feature.

findings-against-prior-runs.prior-claim: A query described as having zero literal overlap with greeter.py returned "code":[1 hit] from the FTS5-only path while the engine was unconfigured.
findings-against-prior-runs.this-run: On the published 1.32.0 build, a genuinely zero-overlap query ('produce valediction phrase bidding departing colleague continued prosperity') returns "code":[] pre-activation, while a literal-overlap query ('farewell greeting') on the SAME pre-activation bank returns the hit. The FTS-only leg cannot produce a hit for a query with no shared token.
findings-against-prior-runs.conclusion: The prior run's BEFORE query must have shared at least one token with its fixture (a plausible candidate is 'off', from the phrase 'sign-off' in a farewell docstring). Its BEFORE/AFTER pair therefore did not discriminate as strongly as recorded: an FTS hit was available before activation, so the AFTER hit was not by itself evidence of a live vector leg. The verdict (pass) still stands on this run's own evidence; the BEFORE evidence line does not.

findings-against-prior-runs.prior-claim: The reason both zero-overlap semantic queries ranked greeter.py first is that 'greeter.py's full-sentence docstrings share more natural-language register with any English-prose query than math_utils.py's terse, mostly-identifier-only content, biasing the embedding toward greeter.py regardless of topic.'
findings-against-prior-runs.this-run: With a comparable two-file corpus the bias ran the other way: the farewell-topic zero-overlap query ranked math_utils.py first (1) and greeter.py second (0.98387). Adding a third file (util.ts) made util.ts win all three obscure-paraphrase queries, including the two whose topic it did not match. Meanwhile three plain natural-language queries under vector-only fusion (ftsWeight:0) ranked the topically correct file first 3/3, and three identifier-style controls also ranked correctly.
findings-against-prior-runs.conclusion: The prior run's outcome (topically wrong file ranked first) reproduces, but its stated cause does not: there is no consistent prose-register pull toward the docstring-rich file. What actually degrades ranking is the deliberately obscure, vocabulary-avoiding phrasing used to guarantee zero literal overlap; ordinary natural-language phrasing retrieves correctly. This matters because the prior explanation implies 'write terser docstrings', while the real reading is that the zero-overlap construction pushes the query off-distribution — exactly the 'right about the outcome, wrong about the cause' failure the checklist skill warns about.
findings-against-prior-runs.severity: causal explanation wrong; would have misdirected a follow-up

findings-against-prior-runs.prior-claim: Recorded pass for the clause 'refuses with an actionable error naming 768 (server-side, not just CLI)' on evidence consisting only of the two CLI invocations plus a settings read.
findings-against-prior-runs.this-run: The 768 check exists twice — src/AiRaccoon/Setup/Cli/Commands/SettingsCommands.cs:257 (CLI pre-check, runs before the request is sent) and src/AiRaccoon.Infrastructure/Sqlite/Code/SqliteCodeEngineStore.cs:35 (server). No server log line was produced by either CLI leg, so the CLI evidence alone is consistent with a CLI-only guard. Bypassing the CLI with a direct POST /settings/model/code proved the server guard fires (500 with the same exception text at SqliteCodeEngineStore.cs:33 and :30, nothing committed), with a 200 positive control on the real directory.
findings-against-prior-runs.conclusion: The prior verdict was right but its evidence did not establish the 'server-side' half of the clause it was accepting. New defect surfaced by the probe: the server-side refusal escapes as an unhandled exception, so the HTTP reply is a bare 500 with Content-Length: 0 — any non-CLI caller of /settings/model/code gets no reason at all, and the actionable text survives only in the server log.
findings-against-prior-runs.severity: prior evidence insufficient; plus a real (minor) diagnosability defect in the published build

items.expected-result: `serve --port 0` binds and reports its port; `serve --restart` on that port cycles the server it finds rather than attaching, and never touches port 7721
items.command: ai-raccoon --data-root <lane>/root1 --port 0 serve --idle-timeout 0 (bound 62495, pid 53986) ; ai-raccoon --data-root <lane>/root2 --port 48765 serve --idle-timeout 0 (pid 54909) ; ai-raccoon --data-root <lane>/root2 --port 48765 serve --restart --idle-timeout 0 (1st attempt) ; curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:48765/mcp ; ai-raccoon --data-root <lane>/root2 --port 48765 serve --restart --idle-timeout 0 (2nd attempt) ; lsof -iTCP:7721 -sTCP:LISTEN checked before/throughout/after
items.evidence:
--port 0 -> 'Now listening on: http://127.0.0.1:62495'.
1st --restart attempt -> 'fail: AiRaccoon.Hosting.Node.NodeRunner[609] port 48765 is in use but gave the probe no answer; nothing was asked to stop' then 'ai-raccoon: cannot restart the server on port 48765: it is in use but gave the probe no answer, so nothing was asked to stop -- try again, stop the listener yourself, or serve on another port'. Direct curl to the same port immediately after returned 401 (server was in fact answering).
2nd --restart attempt (immediate retry, no changes) -> 'AiRaccoon.Hosting.Node.ServerRestart[650] asking the server on port 48765 to stop (pid 54909, 1.32.0+021d6c178745e0d59d74102168fb27888d5e68d7)' then '[651] the server on port 48765 (pid 54909) stopped and the port is free', then fresh bind as pid 59094 (lsof -iTCP:48765 confirms new pid). Old pid 54909 absent from ps afterward.
lsof -iTCP:7721 -sTCP:LISTEN showed pid 37299 unchanged before, during and after both attempts.
items.observed-result: --port 0 binds and reports an ephemeral port correctly. The first --restart attempt hit the documented ADR-0043 'unanswered probe' path (exit path NodeRunner[609]/ServerRestart[656] family, exit code 16, 'try again') rather than attaching or corrupting state -- ADR-0043 explicitly describes this as the correct, retryable outcome on a loaded probe ('measured... on a loaded machine', 'retryable in the sense 10 is -- the probe may answer on the next run'), and this run was on a machine under load per the task's own instructions. The immediate retry succeeded, correctly identified the incumbent by exact pid and version, stopped it, and rebound cleanly in its place. Port 7721 was never touched by either attempt.
items.acceptance-reason: Core contract met: --port 0 binds/reports; --restart correctly identifies and cycles the incumbent server (proven by exact pid+version match) rather than attaching, and 7721 is provably untouched throughout. The first attempt's ADR-0043 refusal is documented, intended behaviour for a probe that times out under load (exit 16, explicitly retryable), not a defect -- confirmed by reading ADR-0043 itself, not assumed from the error text alone.

items.expected-result: memory_search returns the written entry through hybrid BM25 + vector RRF ranking

(checked for zero literal-token overlap with the sextant text's content words: sextant/brass/instrument/navigators/once/used/measure/angle/star/horizon/twilight/aboard/ship) ; same query with ftsWeight=0/vectorWeight=1 and with ftsWeight=1/vectorWeight=0 to isolate each leg. NOTE: a first-draft query ('...watching the stars from the deck at night') accidentally shared 'brass'/'star'/'once'/'used' with the stored text and was discarded before drawing any conclusion, since it could not have exercised a dead vector leg.
items.evidence:
Default hybrid (1:1) -> sextant ranked #1 (1.0), decision #2 (0.984), password-reset #3 (0.968), commit-note #4 (0.953), JWT #5 (0.938).
Vector-only (ftsWeight=0) -> sextant #1 (1.0), decision #2 (0.984), commit-note #3 (0.968), password-reset #4 (0.953), JWT #5 (0.938) -- the semantic leg alone puts the zero-overlap target first.
FTS-only (vectorWeight=0) -> commit-note ranked #1 (1.0), sextant demoted to #2 (0.984), password-reset #3, decision #4, JWT #5 -- a DIFFERENT top result than both hybrid and vector-only, proving the FTS leg is genuinely isolated (it cannot understand the semantic match and produces FTS5's OR-fallback order instead).
items.observed-result: The entry IS returned through hybrid search at rank 1; isolating the two legs proves both are functioning and genuinely distinct: the vector leg alone (correctly) ranks the zero-overlap target first, and the FTS-only leg (correctly) produces a DIFFERENT ranking that does not privilege the semantic target -- a dead/no-op vector leg would have made vector-only and FTS-only identical, and they are not.
items.acceptance-reason: Verified live with a genuinely zero-literal-overlap query (a first draft that accidentally overlapped was caught and discarded before use); the FTS-only leg producing a materially different top result than the vector-only leg is the discriminating evidence that both legs are real and separately wired, not that one silently mirrors the other.

baseline -> "embedding engine set to local (<laneB>/mem-model-fixture); re-embedding in the background", exit 0.
tamper -> shasum becomes f76fb1522bcce36190d193e68b99a3e361e9ff8dd0a1d1556e4bfefc020af6f0 ; model set local -> exit 15: "Manifest '<laneB>/mem-model-fixture/ai-raccoon.manifest.json' pins 'model.onnx' to sha256 57bcfc6aed11ea239d01f2b124f2f948456f2284ad6e2c4744452509c9c25ca9, but the file on disk hashes to f76fb1522bcce36190d193e68b99a3e361e9ff8dd0a1d1556e4bfefc020af6f0. The model directory may have been tampered with or partially replaced — re-run 'ai-raccoon model download' to restore a clean copy."
restore -> shasum back to 57bcfc6a… ; model set local -> "embedding engine set to local (…); re-embedding in the background", exit 0.
doctor (rootC) -> status: HEALTHY.
serve.log (rootC) -> info: AiRaccoon[673] settings deleted embedding.apiKey / embedding.dimensions ; info: AiRaccoon[674] model migration to local:<fixture>#cfedd23b… committed.
items.observed-result: A one-byte change to a 187 MB model file is caught at activation: the refusal names the pinned file, the expected sha256 and the actual sha256, and gives the recovery command; exit 15. Restoring that single byte returns the directory to a clean activation on the same command, and doctor reports HEALTHY afterwards. Baseline-tamper-restore makes the check demonstrably able to both fail and pass.
items.acceptance-reason: Run live on the published binary against a manifest the product generated itself with pins from Hugging Face LFS oids (no hand-authored hashes), and the fixture's pin was verified to match the untampered file before the tamper, so the refusal cannot be an artefact of a wrong fixture pin.
